title: The Stoic day
hookLine: morning preview, attention through the day, evening review

lines: A PHILOSOPHY IN YOUR HEAD IS A HOBBY.
cards: What the Stoics called good, how they saw feelings, their picture of the world, and this week, the Stoics honestly: Musonius arguing for women's education, a slave and an emperor in one school, where they fell short, their real tears, plain food, and Seneca's question.
Big ideas, all of them. But a philosophy that lives only in your head is a hobby. The Stoics wanted it in your calendar, from waking to sleep.
So before we turn to the science, here it all is in one ordinary day.

teach.b: The Stoic day has three parts, and you've met each one on this path. First, the morning preview.

Marcus Aurelius starts book two of his notebook this way, in George Long's translation: "Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial."
It sounds grim, but he goes on: they act this way because they don't know good from bad, and they're my kin, so I can't be harmed by them or angry with them.
It's a weather forecast for people, so the storm doesn't surprise you. Second, attention through the day.

Epictetus has a whole talk on it; the Greek word is prosochē, attention, paying heed. His warning is practical: let your attention slip for a moment, and don't imagine you'll pick it up again whenever you like.
Carelessness today makes tomorrow's carelessness easier. So through the day, the Stoic keeps checking: is this up to me? What am I telling myself?
Is this the jolt, or the yes?
Third, the evening review. Seneca describes how his teacher Sextius, every night before sleep, questioned himself: what bad habit did I cure today? What fault did I resist?
In what way am I better? Seneca does the same, when the lamp is out and his wife has fallen silent, and then he forgives himself and resolves to do better. Morning, you prepare.
Evening, you look back kindly and learn.
None of it takes long, and together they make a whole day into practice.

how: Some modern Stoics keep a short morning reflection, check in with themselves during the day, and write or think through an evening review before sleep.

o: attention, paying heed through the whole day
a morning list of the people you'll meet
the nightly look back at what you did

games.q: the Stoic day — tap the pairs.

s: Marcus's morning preview is meant to make him angry at people
he previews difficult people so he won't be surprised or harmed, and calls them kin.
Epictetus warns that lost attention is easy to pick back up
he warns that slipping today makes slipping tomorrow easier.
Seneca's evening review ends with forgiving himself
he looks back honestly, then forgives and resolves to do better.

games.q: it's the end of a Stoic day, the lamp is out. what does Seneca do?
o: review the day, then forgive himself.
games.why: following his teacher Sextius, he asks what he cured, resisted and improved, then forgives and resolves to do better.

practice: Preview: picture the next few hours, and meet whoever might test your patience kindly, in advance. Attention: come right here, to this breath, and this one.
Review: one thing from today that went well and one to do better; forgive it, and rest.

wordCard.voice: Prosochē, Epictetus' word for attention through the day, alongside a morning preview and evening review: the whole philosophy in one ordinary day.

orig.note: Greek: attention, paying heed; Epictetus's word for the Stoic's daytime practice.

carryVoice: Your line: the whole day. That closes three weeks on the porch; next comes the science of practice. Day three hundred one, complete.

sources.q: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial.
